3. The land was requisitioned with the intent to acquire the same for creating residential plots by Chittagong Development Authority (CDA), by order dated 28-5-64, issued under section 3 of the Requisition of Property Act, 1948. A notice was issued by the Respondent No.2 under section 5(3) of the said Act, for filing objections by the owners of the land on 6-7-68. It is claimed in the petition that the petitioners objected but no one paid any heed and the case lands were acquired under land acquisition case No. 138 of 1962-63. A part compensation was made, though at a very low rate, . and received by the land owners but no final payment has been made nor any final notification issued vesting the said land in the Government. 

 6. With the approval of the Cabinet and on obtaining the opinion of the Ministry of Law and Justice, the Ministry of Land Administration gave a general direction to all the Secretaries concerned by Memo No. DA-72/84/514 dated 30-8-84 (Annexure- B) informing that a decision had been taken that if an acquired land was left unused beyond any justifiable time then it should be released in favour of the original owner without referring to the requiring authority or organisation for whose use the land was acquired. 

 7. By a further memo No. DA-72/84/26-acqn dated 9-12-84 issued by the Ministry of Land Administration and Land Reforms, the Government of Bangladesh reaffirmed the earlier policy for surrendering the unused lands for their utilisation for productive purpose (Annexure-C). Based on the policy of the Government, the said Ministry vide a Memo dated 22-5-86 asked the Deputy Commissioner concerned to send considered opinion whether to release the requisitioned case land in favour of the original owners (Annexure-D). 

 14. It is further stated in the affidavit-in- opposition that the compensation for the lands thus requisitioned was assessed under LA Case No. 138/62-63 based on the prevailing market price of the land in the vicinity then. Therefore, adequate compensation was made over to the original owners as per relevant provisions of Emergency Requisition of Property Act, 1948. It is further stated that no homestead and graveyard were acquired and the land in question is being used based on the Annual Development Programme. 

 16. The grounds taken by the petitioner in the writ petition are that, the impugned order (Annexure G) has been made violating the policy of the Government (Annexure-D). The case land has not been acquired, nor vested, nor full compensation paid, nor used for the purpose for which it was acquired. The land has not yet been vested in the respondents and the petitioners' legal right over the case property is still subsisting as no notification has yet been published in the official Gazette under section 5(7) of the (Emergency) Requisition of Property Act, 1948. The case land includes homestead of the petitioner and family graveyard and thus keeping the land under requisition and declining to derequisition the same by the respondents is a violation of the fundamental right of the petitioners. The (Emergency) Requisition of Property Act, 1948 is ultra vires of the Constitution as it does not provide a clear guideline in it for payment of compensation and, as such, it is incompatible with Articles 36 and 42 of the Constitution. Lastly, the land admittedly having not been used for the purpose for which it was requisitioned for a long period of twenty eight years the continuation of the requisition is not sustainable beyond the life of the Ordinance which was of temporary nature. 

 18. Mr. M Amirul Islam, the learned Advocate for the petitioners, has argued that the requisition and acquisition process of the case land had started in the year 1964, more than twenty eight years back, but so far only part compensation has been paid and the full payment has remained unpaid. Moreover, the compensation is so low that it cannot be considered adequate. But from the record it appears 90% of the compensation money assessed has already been handed over to the original owners and only 10% is yet to be paid. It also appears that the compensation is assessed under LA Case No. 138/62-63 on the basis of the prevailing market price then There is no evidence on record to show that any objection was raised by the petitioners while accepting the 90% of the compensation. Now, after twenty-eight years we do not find any reason for this court in its writ jurisdiction to enter into the disputed question of adequacy or inadequacy of the compensation assessed. 

 19. By referring to Article 42(1) and (2) of the Constitution Mr. Islam next challenged the very vires of (Emergency) Requisition of Property Act, 1948 on the ground that no clear guideline for payment of compensation has been provided in it. Article 42 guarantees that no person shall be deprived of his property by way of acquisition, nationalisation and requisition save by authority of law that provides for compensation and specifies the principle on which, and the manner in which the compensation is to be assessed and paid. We however do not find any substance in the contention of the learned Advocate that the Act does not provide guideline for payment of compensation. Section 5(B) of the (Emergency) Requisition of Property Act, 1948 provides that when a property is requisitioned under section 5(3) with a view to its permanent acquisition, the owner of the property shall be offered or paid in advance before possession is taken over, compensation to the extent of either 100% for structure and building and 90% for lands of the provisional estimate. From annexure F to the writ petition we find that the owners of the case land had already accepted 90% of advance compensation. Moreover, section 7 of the said Act lays down the manner and principle for payment of compensation for immovable property. Sub-section (aaa) of section 7 further provides for arbitration in case of non-acceptance of compensation by the land owners and sub-sections c, cc, d and e of section 7 lay down how an arbitrator shall proceed in calculating the market value of the land requisitioned. From the record it does not appear that the original owners went for arbitration complaining the adequacy of the compensation. 

 "Special Savings Relating to Expired EB Act XIII of 1948. Notwithstanding the cessation of the Emergency Requisition of Property Act, 1948 (EBA XIII of 1948), on the expiry of the period of its operation, all proceedings and matters, including all notices, notifications, and orders, relating to requisition or acquisition of any property or compensation or award in respect of any property requisitioned or acquired and all applications and appeals pending before any authority, arbitrator or court under that Act shall be continued, enforced, heard or disposed of as if that Act had not ceased to have effect and were continuing in operation." 

 27. The learned Advocate for the petitioners then raises the point that the case land has not yet been vested in the Government The original owners are still the legal owners of the case land. Non vesting of the land even after 28 years of requisition shows that the case land is not required for the purpose for which it was acquired. Therefore, the case land should be derequisitioned and returned to the original owners. Here by referring to Sat yam Co-operative Housing Society Ltd. vs. Calcutta Improvement Trust AIR 1989 263 Mr. Amirul Islam argues that the petitioners are well within their right to challenge the requisition for long and inordinate delay by the acquisition authority in concluding the acquisition proceeding. We have gone through the decision and, in our view, the decision referred to is not applicable in the instant case as the facts and circumstances are different. In that case certain land was purchased by a Housing Society and after getting clearance from Calcutta Improvement Trust it started construction of five apartment buildings for its members. While the construction was in progress and a substantial part was completed the Society was asked to stop work and was informed that the acquisition proceeding in respect of the land was pending for a long time. Under the circumstances the Court held that inordinate delay on the part of the acquisition authority can be a cause of action. This is not the case here. Petitioners came to know about the requisition immediately on requisition of the property but neither objected nor went for arbitration rather accepted a substantial part of the compensation.
